225.q: The normal interests as a kid, as a boy – basketball, I'm in sports, what not. I was in the ROTC, in the ROTC band. But a particular interest? No. I don’t believe so. I remember I had a little fling with boxing.

225.s: Johnson and Baker remember Dr. Carroll as an intense, brilliant, humorless teacher of black history.
225.q: He ran a tight ship, a very tight ship. He was a very severe, serious person with no sense of humor whatsoever, [laughs], but a brilliant man.

492.t: USC's focus on Europe and a racist conductor's apology
492.s: At USC Lloyd is told jazz has nothing to do with the curriculum; he plays clarinet in the symphonic band under Shafer, with Shostakovich visiting, and a professor apologizes after Lloyd's band plays.
492.q: And all they wanted to talk about was 300 years of Europe. Now I love Europe and J.S. Bach and Bartok, and all the - Beethoven... I mean I love all that stuff. But I would say, what about prayers and Duke Ellington and Yard and Mr. Armstrong and stuff like that? And Dizz? And then they say, “Well,…

492.s: Lloyd interviews at USC with Stevens, who quietly admits the situation is unfair but offers to work with him on the side.
492.q: So at Christmastime my mother brought me out to Cali from Memphis. I hadn’t graduated yet - this is deep man, this is ’56 - and I interviewed with Halsey Stevens, cause I wanted to study composition with him.

492.s: Lloyd jazzes up Eine Kleine Nachtmusik at his symphonic orchestra audition and the other students laugh.
492.q: Ok? And So Halsey Stevens saw that - cause when I auditioned for the symphony band - symphonic orchestra - I had to audition on clarinet. Well all those little boys who had auditioned before me they said: [Imitates playing Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s Eine Kleine Nachtmusick Movt. 1]. So I said,…

227.t: Schools: PS 9, Tarrytown and New York Military Academy
227.s: Mandel recounts his schooling from PS 9 and Los Angeles public schools to a miserable boarding school at Tarrytown and then the Military Academy on a band scholarship, where he wrote for a dance band.
227.ch: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
227.q: Oh, before that I went to a terrible school that my mother… when I had lost my father; well, I went to grammar schools, public grammar schools in Los Angeles. Actually, first in New York if you’re gonna go all the way back, I went to PS9, where I majored in the Principal’s office pretty much, I was…

227.t: Manhattan School and the collapse of the big bands
227.s: Mandel decided to study after leaving Alvino Rey, as the big bands broke up in late 1946, and says one should learn jazz first.
227.ch: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
227.q: Yeah, I decided there was just too much I didn’t know, too many gaps and I wanted to get off the road. I did for the better part of a year. Went to Manhattan.

227.t: Fighting his way into Manhattan School
227.s: Mandel studied counterpoint and fugue at Manhattan School after camping on its doorstep, with Dick Katz and Russ Savakus as fellow jazz students, and attended a Juilliard summer session.
227.ch: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
227.q: I learned about writing fugues and three voice counterpoint and things like that and kind of took what I wanted and didn’t take what I didn’t. ‘Cause I didn’t like the formalized kind of starchy atmosphere in schools then, Manhattan since then has had wonderful programs.

508.t: Wanting to be a history teacher and uneven grades
508.s: He planned to teach history, earned As in history and English, and ignored math and science.
508.q: Naw. Well I was a good student in the subjects I liked. So I made A’s in history and A’s in English. C’s and D’s in everything else.

508.t: One year at Southern: skipping Harmony I and Batiste sending him away
508.s: He studied history, could not test out of harmony, skipped class, and Batiste and his father decided he should leave for Berklee.
508.ch: Southern, Berklee and becoming a jazz player
508.q: I was going to Southern. I was taking history classes and I was minoring in music. I learned something about like, you know, like…. I mean black schools have a lot of weird issues. Cause I had taken all of these classes at the New Orleans Center for Creative Arts, and I was in a freshman harmony…

508.t: Berklee harmony rules and the piece Shift
508.s: A teacher faulted his composition for breaking Berklee rules, so he wrote a rule-following piece and called it Shift.
508.ch: Southern, Berklee and becoming a jazz player
508.q: rules. So I wrote a piece of music and the teacher said, “Well, this is a very pretty piece of music, but it does not adhere to the Berklee rules for harmony.” “What the hell? Is that what we’re doing here?” So I went and I meticulously wrote this piece that adheres to all the rules the way they…

672.t: School grades and an early taste for suits
672.s: She was an A student except for geometry and home ec, and says she has always preferred suits and trousers to dresses.
672.q: Probably home economics. Something like that. I’m trying to remember what it was. Oh, I remember: geometry. I had A’s in algebra, but I got a C in geometry. And I never did finish the blouse I was working on in home ec.

672.t: Always a singer; choosing work over college
672.s: She never decided to be a singer, would otherwise have gone into medicine, and left Central State after a semester because work was waiting.
672.q: I never did decide to be a singer. I recalled always being one. I don’t recall deciding that I wanted to be a singer. I was always a singer.

672.t: One semester at Central State; Omega sweetheart
672.s: Freshman year she went home weekly, sang little on campus, became an Omega sweetheart and then returned to work.
672.q: When you’re a freshman, you study just a normal – there’s a curriculum that’s already set up. I had not picked a major at that point.

373.s: He describes the oldest public school in America, its tough Depression-era standards and what it taught him.
373.q: Boston Latin School is the oldest public school in the United States: 1635. That was one error that Sandra Day O’Connor made in a Supreme Court decision. She said that there were no public schools until the eighteenth century. She didn’t know about BLS. When I was a kid, I got in on the seventh…

373.t: Visiting Latin's jazz band; Northeastern, the school paper and the First Amendment
373.s: After Jewish quotas at Boston College he went to Northeastern, edited its paper, and quit when the president censored it, sparking his First Amendment interest.
373.q: I stayed there from seventh grade through graduation. By the way, I came back there a few years ago, and to my great surprise, there was a functioning jazz band, which was totally out of possibility when I was a kid. They have a very good bandmaster there. The kids – of course the front line was…

373.t: Leaving Harvard graduate school for Sidney Bechet
373.s: He quit American Studies at Harvard after realizing in Widener Library that Bechet was playing at the Savoy.
373.ch: Black writers, Harvard and Down Beat
373.q: So I decided, that was it. I left.

509.t: Mrs. Nickerson and the avant-garde composition at Howard's Junior School of Music
509.s: Horn corrects the Howard story: Dr. Hughes and her uncle arranged her place, but teacher Mrs. Nickerson crushed her with a composition judged too avant-garde.
509.q: Okay. Well, I was a little shy child, and I was there, and I was in Junior School of Music there, and Dr. Hughes and my uncle, Dr. Horn, set up something special so I could be there, because they thought I was special, right. But this woman, she was . . . I‘m not going to say she was mean. She was…

509.t: Sorting out the chronology at Howard's Junior School of Music
509.s: Stitt untangles her schooling: Howard Junior School at twelve until eighteen, with Shaw and Dunbar; Horn returns to Mrs. Nickerson's criticism.
509.q: Okay, okay. Dr. Hughes and my uncle, Dr. I.B. Horn, started this thing here, in order to make it open for me to do . . . at twelve years old I was in the Junior School of Music, okay. Also, there were people like Frank West, right, and whatever they were doing, I don‘t know, right. But I was there,…

509.t: Accompanying everyone at Shaw Junior High and winning a citywide competition
509.s: At Shaw she accompanied all the singers and shows, and won a citywide competition at thirteen.
509.q: Child, you know one thing. When I was in school, right, see, I was in Shaw Junior High School, there was no one who could play for the specials and stuff like that, but me. I mean, I didn‘t get an education. They had to ship my ass off. I mean, this is, you know, all over the place, all over…

109.t: Washington School and schoolmate Bernard Hilda
109.s: At Washington School he befriended Bernard Hilda, later a Paris impresario and bandleader, who recognised him decades later when Clarke came to Paris with Dizzy.
109.q: I went to the Washington School with a lot of Jewish kids, and one of them is a friend of mine today. He's an impresario here in Paris, and we went to school, when we were about 12 or 13 years old, together.

109.t: Bernard Hilda's move to Paris; Herron Hill High School
109.s: Back to his own schooling: Hilda's family returned to France, and Clarke went on to Herron Hill High School.
109.q: So his father was an ambassador, was a French citizen, though, he had something to do with politics. And they went back -- his father moved back to France and took the family.

109.t: Cal Cobbs and the Wilberforce scholarship
109.s: After two months he returned to Cincinnati to attend Wilberforce on a scholarship arranged by pianist Cal Cobbs, but money problems intervened.
109.q: Yeah. I wanted to come back to Cincinnati, to a friend of mine who was a wonderful piano player. Carl Call Cobbs his name was. And we were supposed to go to university together. What was that university? He had a music scholarship for me.

380.t: Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Shavers at Bordentown; his age at entry
380.s: He mentions that Gillespie and Shavers attended the school, and that he lied about his age to get in at twelve.
380.q: Charlie Shavers and Dizzy Gillespie both went to this school. Dizzy was a bad boy; Dizzy got kicked out of school. He hasn't changed a bit either. Dizzy was always dizzy, you know, kind of a devil, always doing nutty things. But anyhow...

380.t: Bordentown as an industrial school with an intense music program
380.s: He explains that music brought him to Bordentown, where the program ran three hours a day.
380.q: Bordentown, yes. And it just happened to be an industrial school, because they taught agriculture and things like that. But music was what got me there, because the music program was three hours a day, every day, ten

380.t: The school dance orchestra and getting kicked out for smoking
380.s: He led the Bordentown dance orchestra, wanted to play jazz, and explains the demerit system that ended Dizzy's time at the school.
380.ch: Youth, the road and arrival in California
380.q: They had a dance orchestra in school. They had a band and a dance orchestra. And the dance orchestra fell to me, I guess, because I was... There was more than one bass player, mostly tuba players, but I guess I was the one that aspired to Jazz more than the rest of them. The other

93.t: Head of the class and the Constitution newspaper visit
93.s: Newspaper people visit his class; Green talks about the records shop and Tom Bailey's theatre.
93.q: So I finally went up to -- like I was saying, they come up to this school, and whoever was in the head of the class, they would always get chosen to do something, some kind of chore that would be helpful to them in their education.

93.t: Reading his good deeds to the Constitution publishers and a paper job
93.s: Newspaper publishers are impressed by his good deeds, he gets a paper-selling job, substitutes for the teacher and jokes about a late honorary degree.
93.q: Yeah, so again that's what happened. As I say, and I got back into the class. I was in the head of the class again. And these people from the Constitution -- that was the name -- the publishers from the Constitution newspaper were there. And I had to get up. My time came. I got up and read some of…

93.t: Leaving school after eighth grade, Boy Scouts and hospitality
93.s: Green says he went as far as eighth grade, enjoyed performing for neighbours as Southern hospitality, and was educated by his aunt and the radio company school.
93.q: Well, I think I went as far as the eighth grade, see, because I did -- I became a Boy Scout and got in the Boy Scouts --

96.t: Leaving high school; the Maroon Five and a fraternity pledge
96.s: He left school at seventeen, played with college men, and was pledged Delta Tau Delta, wishing for a university education.
96.q: University of Chicago with the Maroon Five. And also went up to Lost Lake with them up in Wisconsin. A bunch of college guys. And I was naturally a highschool boy but I was pledged (Doyta Del Doyta?) and I had you know, visions of going to the University of Chicago. I wanted education naturally.…

96.t: Wanting an education; going to college deans while on the road
96.s: On the Pollack band's one-nighters he asks college deans to let him sit in classes and gets a reading list.
96.q: really realised that the lack of education and I wanted to learn. So I got to go on the road with Ben Pollack's band and orchestra which at that time consisted of Benny Goodman, Glen Miller was also in the band, the Pollack band. And we'd do some one nighters and go around and get up the next day…

96.t: Auditing classes, Plato and Shakespeare, and two years without drink
96.s: He audits classes in towns where he stays, reads philosophy with a dictionary, stops drinking and smoking for two years.
96.q: Well I'd sit in on the lectures and if they had any paper work I would write it down. You know what to do and I'd have to get a book naturally. So I asked the deans. You know, I'd read the books.

112.t: Trouble in public school and the Catholic mission school
112.s: Distracted by show business, he fights on his first day, is moved by his mother to a Catholic school, and cannot be converted.
112.q: Well, these things all excited me. After that, I wasn't much good for education. So, we come back to Philadelphia and I wasn't doing so well in public school. In fact, I went to the public school and the first day I was there, I got into a

112.t: Miss Jordan's singing classes in public school
112.s: Moved to public school, he learns part-singing from a teacher who gives keys with a tuning fork.
112.q: Anyhow, now I'm in the sixth grade -- this is a little later. We have a teacher called Miss Jordan. I'll never forget that. I went to 17th and Pine, to the public school now. My mother took me out of the Catholic school, 'cause she said all I was learning was the 'Hail Mary, full of grace', and she…

112.t: Dropping out for Atlantic City; Jack the Bear versus Eubie Blake
112.s: He leaves school to follow Josephine to Atlantic City and decides Jack the Bear is no match for Eubie Blake.
112.q: So, anyhow, that summer she went to my school, and I was droppin' out of school regular, now. And so far, I was droppin' out of school, but my parents didn't know it because I was leavin' the house with my lunch. And they didn't know I was dropping out, but I was droppin' out, see. And so, that…

150.s: He recounts living in the Irish Channel then returning to Gretna, finishing Hoffman junior high and going on to McDonogh 35 at age 15.
150.ch: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
150.q: Well as I started growing. In the Irish Channel. Yeah well, see I lived in the Irish Channel for I think about three years and then we went back to Gretna. And that's how I happened to start walking after going to high school. See I graduated from Hoffman like around about 35, 36. Then I went to…

150.ch: Irish Channel youth, newspapers and McDonogh 35
150.q: I was, that's when my mother moved back on the west bank of the river, right we were living in Gretna then we had moved out of the Irish Channel.

1024.t: First schools: church school and James Weldon Johnson
1024.q: Well the first school I went to was a church. He called it Makers Church on Conner Street and they was building on J.W. Johnson School, James Wellen Johnson School. Okay. And after the building got completed, well I moved me to the school, you know. I just went to this church, it looked like about…

1024.t: Johnson School, Hoffman and Booker T. Washington
1024.s: Reel two: schools attended and transport, among first group at Booker T. Washington.
1024.q: sisters went to one two yeah we all went to the same school but it didn't come to me with a year and all these you know years but anyway i went there and after i left there i had to i went to after i graduated from there i went to uh hoffman school oh hoffman okay from third and clayborne you know…

22.t: St. Alphonsus school and leaving the prep school after his father's death
22.s: He describes his schooling, the private school he left at 15 when his father died, and abandoned medical plans; the spelling of the school name loops in ASR.
22.q: Yes, I went to St. Alphonsus' Parosal School. That's right down here, just about two blocks from here. Can you spell Alphonsus? A-L-P-H-O-N-S-U-S. Saint. S-T. Yes. And then when I finished there, I went to the university school that was run by Chenet and Dwyer.

22.t: Singing at St. Alphonsus closing exercises
22.s: Asked about the choir, he says he sang counter-melodies to The Holy City at school closing exercises under a teacher named Sokola.
22.q: No, I didn't. But I did sing at the closing exercise. And there was a man who used to teach us there, was named Sokola. His first name, I can't remember. But he used to put on the show for us. And we were singing the Holy City. Ta-da, ta-da, ta-da, ta-da, Hosanna, and so on. And I used to sing…

461.t: Not finishing college; bricklaying while aiming to be a songwriter
461.s: His father made him lay bricks after he quit college; coworkers laughed at his songwriting ambitions.
461.q: No, I studied music aside. Just like I said, as I was getting experience with the band, I began to study music in Harlem. Well, you went to three colleges. No, I went to... I went to Welfelforce University. I went to Southern University of Welfelforce University. I didn't finish college. You didn't…

461.t: Schooling at Southern and Wilberforce, and his first song
461.s: He attended Xavier, Southern and Wilberforce, was suspended over baked potatoes, worked as a mason, and first played Brown Skin, Who You For.
461.q: To Xavier before. Yes, that's when... In... In... In... In... In... Grammar school. I see. Yeah, so naturally, in high school, I went to Wilcox. But in Southern, was it just around seventh, eighth grade, something like that. It's Southern University, just in high school. Starting high school.…

152.t: Schools attended and no music training before the service
152.s: He lists his schools and says he did not start playing until after the army.
152.q: 37. That was, uh, it was on Bienville between Galveston Johnson, one block and the next block from my house. And then there was, uh, uh, uh, McDonough, um, I'm trying to think what it is, Albert Wicker, uh, was, uh, kind of a middle school that was also on Bienville and Durban. And at one time we,…

152.t: Learning of Grunewald through the G.I. Bill and joining Clyde Kerr's band
152.s: He bought a saxophone, enrolled at Grunewald School of Music on the G.I. Bill, and within six months joined Clyde Kerr's band and the black union.
152.q: will we call you? That's not my present wife. Oh, okay. Okay. There you go. Yeah. Yeah. Enough said. Yeah. Okay. So, uh, uh, sometime in December of 45? Uh, yeah, it was, uh, during, in November. I knew it was November. I knew exactly that. Okay. Cause that's when I came home on a furlough. Okay.…

189.t: Returning to Booker T. Washington and graduating
189.s: Went back to high school on discharge, told not to play in the beginner band, graduated 1947.
189.q: no When I went back to Booker T, those kids just learning how to play. And even the principal of the school told me it wouldn't be wise for me to play with these guys because they were just learning. So I didn't have to play with the band.

189.t: Navy concert band and lessons with Gilbert Mitchell
189.s: Davenport recalls the Navy symphonic band and studying privately with Gilbert Mitchell in 1945 before Xavier.
189.q: Well a symphonic band when I was in the Navy. Like a concert band? Yeah. But we didn't have the strings. We didn't have the strings. Well I studied with a guy who played with the New Orleans Symphony Orchestra, Gilbert Mitchell. I studied with him in 55. And I studied with him a good while. That…

876.t: Late start in school at ten
876.s: He never went to school until ten, taught himself playing school, and tested into first grade at a private school.
876.q: No. From the age of around six, seven years old until I was ten, I used to play school on the gut age at night with the kids that went to school. And when I went to school at ten years old, it was a private school. Professor Nixon's aunt and uncle had a school right there, a place called St. James…

876.s: A short aside on his first instrument and how school paused for his first communion.
876.q: Uh, Mm-hm. So she's taking me away from this private school until I made my first communion. I went to school last day, I think about one session. And after I made my first communion, then school closed. It was summer, when I went back to school again. I went back to old-school.

571.t: Schools Lewis attended as a boy
571.s: Lewis recalls how long he was in school and names the schools he attended, leaving at about 12 or 13 to work.
571.q: Well, you started, you started in school about 6 years. You started in 8th school, I think, you know, you just think like that. I went to school when I was about 12, 12, 12, my 13 years, and I was going to go out to work at campus.

571.t: No music at school and where he lived
571.s: There was no music at school, Lewis says he learned little because it was too easy, and he gives his childhood address.
571.q: They used to have a St. Al's Press. They used to have a great job, and they would give grace, and have a whole lunch. And then, what he said, back of your books. He used to have a good deal. And if I lived in the same neighborhood here again, he would send you home probably an hour, half hour in a…

881.t: Schools attended and New Orleans University
881.s: He recounts his elementary schools, a year at New Orleans University, its president, and the vocal music teacher.
881.q: I attended, you see, I, we rented from some people by the name of Lavazzo. So some of our neighbors was, uh, the Champ and B-Sent, the Lavazzo and the Palmers. I remember that very well. And, uh, when I first entered the school, elementary school, I entered in fifth grade, because they had, uh,…

881.t: Schools and religion: New Orleans University and Garden District
881.s: Family religion was part Catholic, part Methodist; he attended New Orleans University and later McDonogh 25 after the family moved.
881.q: Well, no, part of my people, one side a Catholic and the other the Methodist. So I started public school at Tom LeFont School, when I was in 3rd grade. I finished Tom LeFont School and then I, my mother rather, enrolled me in New Orleans University, up at Valmont and St. Charles. Yeah, Bun Johnson…

484.t: Professions and the interviewer's own path
484.s: Small talk about musicians who worked through college, the interviewer's pre-med years and arrival in New Orleans in 1945 with Monk Hazel, and first hearing Harry Shields.
484.ch: Depression years and New Orleans trumpeters
484.q: Many do. Many played their way through universities with black sticks. Mm-hmm. We had a very dear friend during the World War II days in Valparaiso, Florida. One of the men has done a lot of research in the Rubin method of child delivery. He was Dr. Arthur David. He's, he played his way playing…

484.t: School bands, Tulane dances and the theremin
484.s: His band played fraternity dances; for Werlein's he organized school bands and demonstrated the theremin, including for Madame Schumann-Heink.
484.ch: Owls, Werlein's and the OK record
484.q: Oh, yes. Yes, sir. Sure. Why? Well, any place you go in New Orleans, you had a good band. But it looked like we played, the Owls or Brownlee's band would play for so many of the fraternities and sororities of Tulane. And then Loyola, of course, came into the picture after. And we played quite a bit…

510.t: Leaving a biochemistry lab job for music
510.s: He studied medicine and biochemistry at his mother's urging, worked in a cancer lab in Rhode Island while gigging in Boston, and chose music.
510.ch: Early life and path to music
510.q: You know I don’t know. Again, I never really thought about me being a professional musician. You know I went to school and studied medicine. You know my mom wanted me to be a doctor. And I went to a certain point and got my degree in biochemistry, but I got bit. I got bit seriously. I really —…

510.t: Boston years and having no career ambition
510.s: Asked about playing with Chick Corea and Alan Dawson in Boston, he says he never aimed to be a star, just to play his best.
510.ch: Early life and path to music
510.q: No. Never. Never. You know I’m focused in a certain way in terms of let me do the best that I can on this thing. Not what am I going to get from it, endorsements or whatever. Just let me do the best I can and then whatever comes will come. I never — and I don’t know if that was a help or a…

201.s: He auditioned in Boston at 17, won a full scholarship, and left after a year to go on the road.
201.ch: Childhood, Berklee and the Air Force
201.q: Yeah, it’s interesting. Because my mother took me up to Boston, I was 17 years old, and I auditioned for this fellow Ken McKillup, who was like the assistant to Larry Berk. And they gave me a full scholarship. And I can’t remember the details. I had a full scholarship. I didn’t pay any tuition,…

201.t: Leaving Kai, Manhattan School of Music and the first New York jobs
201.s: Sebesky urged him to study; Andre left the group in 1958, used his GI Bill at Manhattan School, and worked at CBS and with Mulligan.

201.q: School of Music.” I don’t know if he said Manhattan, but that’s where he was going anyways. 911.t: Grad school burnout, Texas freedom, and influences Harris and McFerrin
911.s: After comparison burnout in grad school he moved to Abilene Christian, worked on slap tongue freely, and was inspired by Eddie Harris and Bobby McFerrin.
911.q: Oh yeah, yeah. Well a cool thing is that I was able to do it online first in the sense of posting a YouTube video. Yes I had experimented a little bit before. I was teaching down in Texas, Abeline Christian University, I was a full time instructor for six years. And that time was really good for…

911.t: Musical mid-life crisis in grad school and giving up imitating Sonny Rollins
911.s: A younger student outplayed him, he wanted to be Sonny Rollins, then realized he should play how he wants; musicians should be honest about what they like.
911.q: Yeah well I mean I had like a kind of musical mid-life crisis in grad school, that period where I was working really hard but kind of burning out at the same time. And it came from, I specifically remember the moment. I was second year grad school — I was a grad assistant so I was supposed to be…

506.t: Eastman had no jazz program; first African American in the Philharmonic
506.s: Eastman recognized jazz but did not teach it; Carter was the first African American in the Eastman Philharmonic and first bassist in the student ensemble.
506.q: In the Eastman Philharmonic I was the first African American in the orchestra, and when they put together what’s now known as the Eastman Philharmonic School Ensemble, it was composed of the better players of the school at that time, that would be my last year, ’58, ’59; and when they put together…

506.t: Enrolling at Manhattan School of Music and studying with Robert Brennand
506.s: He delays a scholarship until January 1960, enrolls for a master's, and studies with the New York Philharmonic's first bassist.
506.q: I applied for a scholarship and I didn't think I was gonna get it, so I was in New York, let's just try to go to school again. So, I got the scholarship and I was supposed to enroll in Manhattan September '59. Well, I had a gig to be on the road, so I talked them into letting me delay the…

926.t: Walter Dyett and DuSable High School
926.s: Davis's main education was Walter Dyett at DuSable, a teacher rather than a jazz teacher.
926.q: Well this was from DuSable High School in Chicago, where a lot of musicians from Chicago were guided by this individual. Most musicians who came out of Chicago went to this high school. And he had a formula that musicians adapted to it, and became fairly successful behind it. I found that.

926.t: Chicago schools: Milt Hinton, Dyett and Wendell Phillips
926.s: Milt Hinton and Dyett's history at Wendell Phillips with Nat Cole and Dinah Washington.
926.q: No, he’s a little ahead of my time. But we have talked about Chicago on a number of occasions, because he informed me of some aspects of Walter Dyett. Walter Dyett used to teach at a school, in fact Walter Dyett taught him. He was in school with Nat King Cole and Dinah Washington, and his school…

754.t: Entering Berklee on a rehabilitation scholarship
754.s: Asked how he learned what he was doing, Galper says he understood nothing until Berklee, which he attended on a state scholarship because he has one eye.
754.q: Not until I went to Berklee. The last year of high school there was a thing in Massachusetts at the time, a State Rehabilitation Board which went around to all the high schools. They would support/help people who were disabled. And since I had one eye I qualified for a scholarship to Berklee. And…

754.t: Berklee's status and the later Artist's Diploma
754.s: He did not graduate in his time at Berklee; years later, through Herb Pomeroy, he got an Artist's Diploma and the school soon dropped its DownBeat ads.
754.q: I didn’t stay long enough to graduate. I graduated much later, many years later. It’s a long story but Berklee never recognized my contributions. And I’d been noticing at the time DownBeat was having all these ads, one page ads, with pictures of their graduates,

486.t: Don Ewell, North Carolina college band, Navy and move to New York
486.s: Ewell's style, joining a Basie-stock college band at the University of North Carolina, Navy band service, then New York and Manhattan School of Music.
486.q: a contemporary, what was then contemporary. He used to sound a little like Teddy Wilson and Jess Stacey. That was contemporary when he came up. But then after the war he went back and he became like Jelly Roll Morton. He was not original but he was identifiable. In other words the idea is if you’re…

486.t: Juilliard rejection and Janet Schenck at Manhattan School
486.s: Katz is turned away at Juilliard but admitted to Manhattan School by Janet Schenck; Teddy Wilson teaches jazz piano at Juilliard.
486.q: teaching a course of jazz piano at Juilliard. The only one. It wasn’t a course it was like three or four guys that you’d go in and you’d play for him and it was almost like individual lessons with just a few. And I guess he was there because of his name, I don’t know, because there was no jazz…

560.t: Western Kentucky University, Bowling Green gig and senior recital
560.s: He chose Western Kentucky on Cannonball's advice, worked a five-night gig, studied counterpoint with Claude Rose, and learned to finish a job through his senior recital.
560.q: I wanted to not go to college and just play, but my parents really balked at that and so my dad insisted that I go to college. And so my grades went — I was working for some obscure college up in the mountains someplace, and I happened to choose Western Kentucky University. And Cannonball was…

560.s: Overton's assignments, started when Longo felt he knew nothing despite a Down Beat write-up, began showing up in his playing, making him a counterpuntalist.
560.q: And the first lesson I had with him I had just been written up in Down Beat, Dizzy’s pianist and all this. And I went and I took a lesson with Hall and I said, “I don’t know anything.” I walked out of there feeling all dejected. I said here I am in DownBeat magazine and I don’t know anything man.…

811.t: Declining Berklee and starting business school
811.s: Accepted to Berklee with a full ride in 1976, he stays in Michigan at Eastern Michigan as a marketing major while gigging.
811.ch: College and the road to jazz
811.q: Oh yeah. I graduated high school in Ann Arbor, Michigan in 1976 and was accepted at Berklee College of Music in Boston, and placed in the number three big band as a freshman. That was like what? Okay. I guess I’m pretty good at what I’m doing here, and I’d love to go to Berklee and be a musician.…

811.t: Flunking out, William Paterson, the cassette and Basie's call
811.s: He flunks out, returns as a music major, transfers to William Paterson, sends a cassette to Grover Mitchell and gets a call from Count Basie.
811.ch: College and the road to jazz
811.q: Yeah. You know, drinking and smoking pot and girls and all that stuff, and I was just happy going to band and playing gigs along the way. And I said hey, this isn’t terrible. Forget those classes. So eventually technically I flunked out of Eastern Michigan. So I laid off a semester and went back on…

656.t: Getting through school: Sam Scamacca, music classes and the school big band
656.s: Teacher Sam Scamacca excused him from early classes and gym if he got 100 on tests; they ran variety shows with Ronnie Foster and others, and he played Taps.
656.q: Once in a while. She threw water on me a couple of times. She actually did that a couple of times. “You’ve got to get up, you’ve got to go to school.” So then I got a pact with, again, one of the major influences in my life was Sam Scamacca, my high school.

656.t: John Sedola's strict lessons and the football ultimatum
656.s: Teacher John Sedola demanded six hours of practice a week; after a sprained finger he made Militello choose between football and lessons, and the coach later conceded.
656.q: Yes. Right. His whole thing was in the lesson you only sound like him. He doesn’t want you to sound like you or anyone else. You sound like him only. And the idea was that he was teaching you an embouchure control situation that when you really had it down and you knew what you were doing could…

586.t: Being a bassist at a sports-minded high school
586.s: Rose describes her place in a sports-based high school and her many roles in the music department.
586.ch: Taking up bass and high school
586.q: Well I mean I came from a very sports-based high school too. So a lot of people weren’t very supportive of the music department except for the people in there. But I think they thought it was really interesting. I mean there’s this huge instrument and you know I had been doing really well playing,…

586.t: Twenty MVP awards at high school competitions
586.s: She won twenty MVP awards in competitions from sophomore to senior year, which gave positive reinforcement.
586.q: Right. At school every year we do maybe six competitions, that type of thing. And since my sophomore year, to my senior year, the first one in my sophomore year, I received an MVP, 20 of them, yeah. So it was great. It really helps. It was a positive reinforcement for me to keep playing and trying…

943.t: North Texas State and switching to an English major
943.s: Soph recalls North Texas in 1963-68 before jazz degrees, why he left music for English, and his timpani hopes.
943.q: Yeah I switched, became an English major in my junior year. Let me — how to put this — I knew I wanted to play music but I realized that the degrees as set up at North Texas at that time really had nothing to do with what I wanted to do musically other than getting me the great opportunity of…

943.t: Houston sessions, St. Thomas High and Harry Lantz's youth orchestra
943.s: Houston drummers and clubs, his parochial high school and the youth orchestra under Harry Lantz.
943.q: with a lot of good drummers: Malcolm Pinson; a great drummer named Carl Lott who’s still alive, a great drummer; Richie Lockwood, I don’t know what happened to Richie. But man, and there were at least four or five full time jazz clubs in Houston back then.

501.s: Spellman is not a musician; he studied voice in college and turned to poetry.
501.q: I studied voice as an elective in college. I had a very good voice but no talent for singing. Nobody ever got mad at me for singing but nobody — I didn’t get notes from the ladies at the bar asking me to come over for a drink either. So nobody ever gave me big

501.t: Leaving Elizabeth City for Howard and meeting Baraka
501.s: Decided to be a poet; left for Howard in 1952 for pre-med, met LeRoi Jones, and the hat story. Acting in He Who Gets Slapped; committed to poetry by junior year.
501.q: No. Not at all. I did not at all think about making a living. I just thought that I wanted to write. I didn’t want — I left home, left Elizabeth City, North Carolina in 1952 to go to Howard University to study to be pre-med. The high school I went to in Elizabeth City was really very poor and…

852.t: Junior high tuba, first improvisation, and being recruited back into band
852.s: Watkins debated his future, learned basic improvisation from the band director, left band out of his high school signup, and was pulled back by the principal and band director.
852.q: I was having a debate with myself. Because I spent, you know band was important to me developmentally, as it is for a lot of students, musicians coming up through school. And I was in junior high and I was going through a little bit of a misbehavior phase as well because I remember myself and my…

852.t: Marching band sousaphone and Joseph Daley
852.s: Talk of sophomore-year marching band and sousaphone, and a mention of tuba player Joseph Daley.
852.q: Joseph Daley, yeah, yeah, yeah. I’m a fan.

61.s: Learned English at Hunter College Model School, saw 'Babe smacks 26, 27', took up sports and dropped piano.
61.ch: Boyhood, Armenian roots and first loves
61.q: Back up, then we’ll pick up – it was the Hunter College Model School that – oh, I know. I was going to talk about how I found baseball.

61.t: Brother Al, Jack Kerouac and the Horace Mann archives
61.s: Al took Kerouac to jazz clubs; Kerouac interviewed Avakian, so the school archive holds both his Goodman and Kerouac interviews.
61.ch: Erroll Garner and the long-playing revolution
61.q: Yes, that’s right, before that. We’ll talk about it, maybe. You coming back tomorrow? The business about LPs and how I was able to sneak jazz in, because essentially that was what happened. I was about to tell about the signing of Erroll Garner for this piano series. Erroll came into it in an odd…

1.t: Nelson Medard's private school and its rattan discipline
1.s: Barker attended Medard's private school at Burgundy and Barracks with future musicians Emile Labat and George Guesnon and recalls the beatings and the lunch his wife served.
1.ch: Old New Orleans musicians and schooling
1.q: I went to Medard school. I went to private school from kindergarten . . . not kindergarten . . . from first grade through the second grade.

1.t: Marigny School and Medard's wife's punishment of girls
1.s: After two years Barker moved to Marigny School, and he recounts being whipped for peeking at the girls' punishment and learning bits of French and Spanish.
1.ch: Old New Orleans musicians and schooling
1.q: On Marigny Street. Marigny between [North] Villere [Street] and [North] Robertson [Street]. There’s a little project-like building up in there now.

526.t: Lutheran school and music only from home and church
526.s: She went to a Lutheran school after a fight at public school, liked drawing letters and music, and had no school music program.
526.q: School yes. I went to a Lutheran school. They wanted me to go to a religious school, but not a Catholic school. In my religion Catholics were sort of mystical, and too weird. So, the Lutherans were a little mystical and weird too, but that’s the school that they put me in, until I guess the sixth…

526.t: Skipping school for the zoo and the dishwasher training school
526.s: She left school at fifteen, having spent her days at the zoo, and was sent to a job-training school that identified her as a dishwasher.
526.q: I was fifteen when I left. It wasn’t legal to leave at that age. So I had to go to a school for people who had dropped out early, which was teaching you to be a dishwasher or something. There’s a word for that, what kind of a school is that? Teaching a person domestic work... I forget the word.

105.s: He majored in English hoping to be a writer and, with Dexter Gordon, earned an A from the toughest English teacher.
105.q: You know what, in school I majored in English. I was going to be a writer. Dexter Gordon and myself were the only two guys, Hambone (unintelligible); we had the toughest English teacher in the whole entire school -- Jefferson. We were the only three dudes that got -- I got an A in English, man,…

105.t: Schools attended and buying his own clothes
105.s: He went to Nevins, Lafayette Junior High and Jefferson High, and by 11 was buying his own clothes with shoeshine money.
105.q: I was working, man. Let me tell you something, man. When I graduated from junior high school, I started buying my own clothes when I was 11 years old.

110.t: Early schooling, the slow group and possible dyslexia
110.s: He recalls kindergarten, being put in the slow reading group, trouble with spelling and reading music, and his Army IQ score; ends with a short break.
110.ch: Family and boyhood in Concord and Ione
110.q: I started in kindergarten at Willow Grammar School in Concord. I guess it was called Willow Pass Grammar School. I can remember the kindergarten. The teacher there was Miss Burns. She and I were in love. Just great.

110.t: Wanting to be a cowboy and going to College of the Pacific as pre-med
110.s: He did not want college; he left military academy after half an hour, dreamed of the Blakely Ranch, and agreed to study veterinary medicine at Pacific.
110.ch: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
110.q: I didn’t want to go. My father had given me four cows when I graduated from grammar school. He kept those cows in his herd, but kept books on how they reproduced and what I owned. I thought I was going to be a cattleman.

470.t: Strengths and gaps in his school music training
470.s: The school gave good theory and ensemble training but lacked strings, bassoons and up-to-date equipment.
470.ch: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
470.q: Yeah. There was a lot of activity. We had a really strong music department, so I had a lot of good training. There were a lot of things I didn’t get. An orchestra in a black school at that time probably would not have had much in the way of strings. We didn’t have any bassoons during the whole time…

470.t: Jazz as an extracurricular activity and Ernst Hoffman's Till Eulenspiegel remark
470.s: Jazz was not part of the School of Music curriculum, and Baker recalls Hoffman correcting his Straight No Chaser practice with the Till Eulenspiegel melody.
470.ch: College, Los Angeles and Lincoln University
470.q: Yeah. We had – as all the other schools, anything you did was extracurricular if it was jazz. It was sometimes accepted, but more often than not it was against the grain of what was happening, because people tend to protect those things which they value most highly. Classical music was one of the…

504.t: Correcting the record on the Chicago Conservatory
504.s: He only took private piano lessons there and never graduated.
504.ch: Faith, study and the Chicago scene
504.q: The Chicago Conservatory, I took private lessons there. It has been said that I graduated from there, somehow that got put down in my historical records. That is not the case, I did not graduate from there. I took some private lessons with some good

504.t: Joseph Jarman joke and leaving Wilson College
504.s: A light aside on Jarman's marriage, then confirming he stayed only a semester before committing to music.
504.q: Because then I decided I'm just going to go sink or swim with music. Being a full time musician.

143.t: Precocious student, paper boy, baseball, off to A&T
143.s: He graduated at 15 as valedictorian, memorized Yankee lineups from the sports page, and went to North Carolina A&T.
143.q: Well, I was...what you call it...a precocious guy. I checked everything out. I could tell you right now New York Yankees in 1936.

143.t: North Carolina A&T and its band
143.s: A&T had no music degree, but he played marching and semi-classical music in the band.
143.q: Well, it was an agricultural and technical school. They didn’t have a music department. I mean, they had a music department, but they didn’t have a music degree. But I got into the band, and got to play in it, so I was all right.

116.t: Failing eighth grade and English teacher Margie Sarter
116.s: He fell behind, loved English and was introduced to Black poets by his teacher.
116.q: I didn’t really excel in anything. When I got to the eighth grade – this was a school in the city of New Orleans, I had spent two years at this school in Shrewsbury, and I was so far behind, I failed the first semester. But I always did like English, and I think when I finally had begun to figure…

116.t: Gilbert Academy and finishing high school
116.s: He attends the Methodist Gilbert Academy, then finishes at another school after the building is sold.
116.q: In the eighth grade. The following year I graduated and went to high school, the Methodist school, Gilbert Academy. I liked that school. It was more like a community, and the principal was the wife of a Methodist bishop. She was sort of like a mother hen with biddies. It was the same high school…

527.t: Leaving Los Angeles in 1946 and the diploma left in the principal's safe
527.s: He left before the school year ended and the principal kept his diploma in a safe for ten years.
527.q: Yeah, well, that’s another story [laughs]. You see, what happened was that the year was coming to an end, and I was supposed to get my diploma. I know my mother wanted that diploma, so I went to the principal and told the principal, “What’s happening is that I have this chance to start my career. I…

527.t: Addison after McShann and his Juilliard scholarship
527.s: Addison settled in the Bay Area, then studied bass in New York and won a Juilliard scholarship, which Art opposed.
527.q: Well, we worked our way back to California with McShann’s band, and then he got a gig up in the Bay Area, and he moved up there. He was working very much up there, and I’m in LA working at the LA General Hospital and whatever else I could get.

134.t: Chicago homes, Willard School and getting into DuSable
134.s: He lists his addresses, being moved to Burke School to graduate, and using his great-aunt's address to get into DuSable and Captain Dyett's band.
134.q: Yeah, always. I was born on the west side of Chicago – I forget that address – and moved to 4909 Champlain Avenue on the south side, which is where I was until I was – went to Willard Grammar School [Frances Willard Elementary School], and I stayed there until – I almost graduated from Willard, but…

134.t: Dyett's discipline and Freeman's debt to him
134.s: Freeman credits Dyett with his musical intellect and describes his strictness and background, as Coleman notes a teacher of his also studied with Dyett.
134.q: We fooled around and played around. Walter Dyett was so great, until he just put up with all of this stuff and still tried to get you to learn the correct embouchures and to learn how to read correctly. Actually I gave him all the credit in the world, because we were all just full of nonsense,…

371.t: Schools attended and playing marches at Bagley School
371.s: Bagley Grade School, Washington Junior High and Pontiac High School; he played marches at recess.
371.ch: Pontiac childhood, family and piano training
371.q: Yes, there was always music. Yes, in the Bagley School, I used to play during the recess, when all the kids would go out to recess, to go march out for recesses, I’d play them marches to come back in. (sings a march tune) This was in grade school. I didn't end junior high school but in grade school…

371.t: High school music appreciation teacher Arnold Warziel
371.s: A high school teacher taught him to listen to symphonies and identify instruments; a Spanish club.
371.ch: Pontiac childhood, family and piano training
371.q: There was a teacher in high school named Arnold Warziel. I think he inspired me more than any other teacher I’ve ever had though. He got us to listen. I was taking a music appreciation course and he got us to listen to the symphonies and the ballets and identify the instruments and identify the…

16.s: Failing mathematics at City College, he got his parents to pay for Juilliard through Carrie B. Overton's help, entering a music education course.
16.ch: City College, Juilliard and early bands
16.q: How'd I get to Juilliard. I got to Juilliard this way. I was playing as I told you, playing music with Leonard Ware and his trio and with various people going around all this time during high school days. I happened to have gotten a hundred percent in a geometry regents in high school and I thought…

16.t: What Juilliard gave him and Ellington's first job
16.s: Juilliard (1938-42) gave him working knowledge of every instrument and a degree; Ellington gave him his first job after graduation and called him his classical arm.
16.ch: City College, Juilliard and early bands
16.q: In retrospect I'd say it has an enormous effect. First of all, it gave me a working knowledge, cursory though it may have been in certain things, but a working knowledge of every instrument in the band because I was to be expected to teach these beginning courses in each one of those things, you…

451.t: Studying theory at the Institute; the harp grade; deciding to go to L.A.
451.s: He nearly went to another school, got into the Institute, earned a theory degree, began a master's, and left after a bad grade when a friend offered a ride west.
451.q: Yeah, there was no guitar and no, no jazz at all. I mean, taught in the school. In fact, I had… I could of… I had started… I was gonna go to a different school and major in English ‘cause I was also interested in that. I can’t think of the name of that school. And then I saw my curriculum and there…

451.ch: Group playing, Town Hall and the White House
451.q: I don’t… it might have been. I don’t think so because there was no guitar originally in that… that was my… when I was in music school. It was a string quartet.

471.s: He attended St. Augustine's from kindergarten through ninth grade, walked there, remembers a girl who escorted him and a neighborhood bully.
471.ch: Growing up and learning drums in Washington
471.q: Yeah, it’s right in there somewhere. I’m trying to think. Yeah, it’s right there. I used to walk – be able to walk to school from wherever we were living at the time. I remember that. The teachers – sisters always - I remember them being nice and kind to me, the Dominican sisters, I think they call…

471.t: Armstrong High School and the drum and bugle corps
471.s: He went to Armstrong, the vocational school across from Dunbar, and joined the drum and bugle corps.
471.ch: Growing up and learning drums in Washington
471.q: That was in Armstrong High School. That’s the school that Charlie Rouse went to. It’s a technical school. It wasn’t like a – it was right down across from Dunbar.

460.s: Laws says he made straight A's, recalls a teacher who paid a dollar per A, and says the teachers and principal were all black.
460.q: I was straight A’s. There was – I’m trying to think of that name, that woman – that teacher. She always – [Wineffie?] gave us a dollar for each A we made. So I wanted to get those dollars.

460.t: Curtis rejection and winning the Juilliard scholarship
460.s: After a failed Curtis Institute audition, Laws finds a Local 47 notice for a Juilliard scholarship and wins it. The scholarship covered tuition only.
460.ch: Modern Jazz Sextet, the flute and Los Angeles
460.q: To tell you the truth, I had just come back from an audition. I got on a train. Went all the way to Philadelphia to audition at the Curtis Institute. The reason why I did that is because my teacher told me, “You could make it in a breeze.” Okay? So, I got – I was in a breeze, too. Going on that…

589.t: An average student drawn to math and science before music
589.s: He was an average student interested in how things work until Mendelsohn turned him to music.
589.ch: Growing up on the Near North Side
589.q: Until Dorothy Mendelsohn, around 12 years old, piqued my interest in piano playing, I thought of math, I thought of science. Fortunately, before I had to decide, make a decision, Dorothy Mendelsohn came into my life, and it became music. My grades were average. I wasn’t an exceptional student at…

589.t: Correcting the record: studying with Mendelsohn at Roosevelt and DePaul
589.s: He did not finish a DePaul degree but followed Dorothy Mendelsohn to DePaul after she left Roosevelt.
589.q: No. Dorothy Mendelsohn left Chicago Musical College, which became Roosevelt University. When it became the university, I think she stayed there a minute, and then she went to teach at DePaul University. I followed her. So DePaul owns me. Roosevelt University owns me.

505.t: Queens College to NYU: majoring in history
505.s: He left a music major at Queens after the Palestrina-to-Stockhausen listening list and finished a history degree at NYU while living a second life downtown.
505.ch: College and the New York scene
505.q: I went first year to Queens College. I stayed. I didn’t want to leave New York, because of the music. By then I knew that there’s no way to go anywhere else and still do anything to do with this. I got into a couple schools. I was on the waiting list at Brandeis, I remember, and I said to my…

505.t: Not being a music major: the value of a college education
505.s: Kirchner and Liebman compare English and history degrees to music study; Liebman says his degree shaped his thinking though he felt late to the New York scene.
505.q: I definitely have a view on this, big time, because when I was in the midst of it, I really was very upset, because I said – first of all, remember in our time there wasn’t a jazz program. But the fact that I didn’t even do music, because after that Queens College debacle with the required…

686.s: He spent his Berklee time finding ways into the studio, using invented names to book it until the school cracked down.
686.q: I had become not so good a student by that point. Early on, I was a straight-A student, but by the time I got to Berklee, I had an idea what I wanted to do. Berklee was not really the – Berklee’s not a very regimented – no, no. Let me say it a different way. Berklee treats you as an adult. They…

686.t: Correcting the record on English studies at UNO
686.s: He enrolled in master's-level English classes to prepare to write operatic works, but left to tour.
686.ch: Sideman years: Fats, Ibrahim, Blakey, Elvin
686.q: I went back and enrolled in classes, because I was interested in – I wanted to write things that are more in an operatic vein. So I figured I wanted to fine-tune my English, my understanding of the language and the writing. So I went back and studied on the masters level for three semesters.

228.t: School days to Roosevelt High, and Sonny Rollins at Stitt Junior High
228.s: McLean walks through P.S. 113, P.S. 46, Stitt Junior High where he first heard Sonny Rollins, Benjamin Franklin and Roosevelt High to follow Andy Kirk Jr.
228.ch: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
228.q: My first schooling, I remember, was a little brown schoolhouse which was in a church on – around 137th Street and Bradhurst [Avenue], one of those churches over there by St. Marks Baptist Church. I went there for a while. Then I went to P.S. 46 – no, P.S. 113, which was on 113th Street between…

228.t: Going back to Greensboro for college in 1954
228.s: To please his mother he went to North Carolina A&T though he had already recorded with Miles; he met Dannie Richmond's circle and T. J. Anderson.
228.ch: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
228.q: I came back to go to school, to try to go, to please my mother, who wanted me to go to college, even though I had already recorded with Miles.

114.t: Reading and Newark; mistaken for deaf and sent to a school for the deaf
114.s: Raised in Reading, then Newark; his hearing loss was misread as slowness, he was placed in a school for the deaf, and he later went to Arts High School.
114.q: Oh, yeah! Yeah. And we were living in Reading, Pennsylvania when my mother was pregnant and -- and, you see, we weren't living in Savannah, Georgia.

114.t: Growing and changing; no real schooling; his mother as his anchor
114.s: Moody talks about change and environment, getting an F in music at Arts High School, learning little in school, and crediting his mother and books.
114.q: You know. I just didn't like it. Now, I've heard Take Six [phonetic sp.], I love gospel music! That time -- kind, you see, because for me, it's okay to be crude, but crudeness can only last for so long. After a little while, you gotta get a little better. If you keep on with the same thing, I'm…

367.t: Francois puts him on first trumpet; Wilberforce offer and running away
367.s: Francois falls out with older brother Granville but puts young Snooky on first trumpet; his mother refuses the Wilberforce offer and he later runs off to join Chick Carter.
367.q: He played piano. Well, that‘s what he played; he played piano. Well, he was a music teacher there at this school and he took a likening to my brother and me. My brother also played trumpet.

367.t: Dunbar High School and teacher Clarence Francois
367.s: Young recalls Dunbar High, its coach Slater and music teacher Clarence Francois, a pianist.
367.q: Integrating, exactly. Going to other schools, but I never did, I stayed on the west side, I went to Dunbar High School. They had some great teachers there, I thought. Francois, was the musician teacher at the school, Clarence Francois, you might have heard of him. The coach for the school, he was…

102.t: Peabody voice lessons with Mrs. Campbell
102.s: A white Peabody teacher crossed the color line weekly to teach him voice, told him to give up boxing and football, and he feared hugging her.
102.q: the deal was blacks were not allowed to go to Peabody in those days. So, there was a white teacher who would break the color barrier each week and she would come to an all black school and teach me to sing. That was my first professional training. This woman, she was really very good. Early on, at…

102.t: Arguing with Peter Mennin about jazz at Juilliard
102.s: He challenged composition teacher Peter Mennin on Juilliard ignoring jazz, won the class with J.J. Johnson's sound, and credits Wynton Marsalis for later change.
102.q: Oh, man! I got in a big argument, a huge argument, with a man who was going to become President of Juilliard. He was in charge of a certain section. One day, I was put in a class with composers and all of them were subjected to this teacher who was a composer himself, brilliant, Peter Mennin. So,…

80.t: Church choir, brass band and the only graduate of the cadet school
80.s: He kept playing in the church choir and brass band at conventions; of 50 boys he alone continued, until boarding school.
80.ch: Boyhood in Evergreen and Calhoun school
80.q: Well, then, as far as I can say, then I'd start -- I was playing in the church choir and then playing in the brass band because we'd go -- they took us here and there for different, say, conventions, you know, take the entire band, and, as I was saying to you, we had this blackboard -- had 50 young…

80.t: Calhoun boarding school and the blacksmith shop
80.s: Calhoun, a Tuskegee-affiliated school in Alabama, let students work; he learned blacksmithing alongside academic subjects.
80.ch: Boyhood in Evergreen and Calhoun school
80.q: That was also in Alabama. That's the name of the little town, Calhoun. That's about -- that was not too far, well, 27 miles below Montgomery, and it was a subsidiary of Tuskegee. It was, you know, connected.

230.t: Sorting out the order of his schools and school bands
230.s: Barnet and Willard untangle Berkeley-Irving, Riverdale, Blair, New Trier; he played tuba at Blair and soprano at Riverdale.
230.q: No, on the contrary. I mean I was very happy with the school, but I liked New York. This was at the time just a little bit too rural for my tastes. Because It was quite rural at that time. Now I guess it's all built in like everything else is.

230.s: Clarifying that he attended Rumsey Hall in Connecticut at about 11, where there was no band.
230.q: Oh, that was very early. I went there one year. That was up in Connecticut. That was sometime -- I would say that was between Burkley Irving and Riverdale.

113.t: Scholarship to Knoxville College and the stop at Fisk
113.s: He and Jesse Culbertson got scholarships to Knoxville College in Tennessee and rode with Culbertson's uncle to Nashville, where his old teacher urged them to stay at Fisk.
113.ch: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
113.q: I wanted to go to college. Well, I had a chance to go to Knoxville College, which is in Tennessee, and so there was another fellow there --

113.ch: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
113.q: Well, I always had a -- wanted to go to school. I don't know why I had it, you know, but I did, and so I went to junior college.

68.t: Schools in Sherman and Booker Pitman
68.s: He attended Frederick Douglass High; he discusses Booker Pitman and Budd Johnson.
68.q: The schooling? We had the schools. I went to Fred Douglass High. That was one of our black leaders, you know, a slave. And Booker T. Washington. Now that was Booker Pitman's grandfather, who was a great saxophone player at one time. I used to play with him. He died in South America. He came up --…

68.t: Wiley College scholarship and the order of his early bands

68.q: : Yeah, I did. You see, I finished. Then I didn't go to college until maybe after I'd been playing with Holder. You know, I didn't until I got a chance to -- I was playing with Holder. 378.t: A few months at Illinois, then the call to join the Collegians
378.s: After starting at the University of Illinois he leaves in November 1925 when Jack Tebo calls about vaudeville act The Collegians; Dance asks what he planned to study.
378.q: So, in the FALL, after that tour was over, I went to Champagne. And I really enjoyed it. I went home for a couple of days and then went over to the University of Illinois and registered, started. Well, in November I get a call from this same Jack Techo, who's producing an act called The Collegians,…

378.t: Quitting school for the Marigold Ballroom; his mother's visit
378.s: Fed up in the speakeasy, Norvo calls Jack Tebo, who gets him a job directing the Marigold band in Minneapolis; his mother comes to visit just as he is leaving.

378.q: Was in that band, and they'd come inbetween shows, maybe -- so I was there -- Wefland said, 'Wait, you said "No." come back, you don't want to (unintelligible), so I went out and had something to eat and I came back was going to meet him. 89.t: Solfeggio from first grade and its payoff later
89.s: Ohio schools taught sight singing from first grade, and it still let him outdo conservatory students in Puerto Rico.
89.q: In grade school, the very first year in school you were taught do, re, me, fa, sol, la, ti, do, and the pitch and the value. To this day I can look at a note now and know the pitch before I play it.

89.t: Wilberforce University and meeting Claude Jones and Edgar Hayes
89.s: After high school in Pittsburgh he attended Wilberforce, played in the band and met trombonist Claude Jones and pianist Edgar Hayes.
89.q: Well, yes. I came back and they decided then that I should go to -- I got through my high school. I went to Pittsburgh to high school and I came back from there and I went to Wilberforce University. And I met a lot of guys there and I was also in the band there and met the great Claude Jones who…

232.t: Bostic and West at college, Luther West's draft, and the Catholic teacher Freeman
232.s: Bostic at Creighton, West at Xavier, West's induction and Love's 1943 call from Fields; Mr. Freeman taught both boys.

232.q: One or the other. He's from Tulsa too. He came here and West, they weren't exactly the same classmates, very close, but West went to Xavier in New Orleans.

232.t: Wanting to be a mechanic and choosing Tuskegee
232.s: He dreams of baseball and auto mechanics, hears one can work one's way through Tuskegee, and ends up studying applied electricity; his brother, a Tuskegee band trumpeter, kids him.
232.q: That was really my first real teacher. But I still wanted to go away and as I said, I never did think about music as a livelihood, and I wanted to be an auto mechanic; baseball and auto mechanic was my dream. I could just listen to the old cars and tell you what was wrong by the sound it was making.

29.t: Steubenville High School and its band
29.s: Howard says he graduated from Steubenville High School, where he played tenor sax in the school band.
29.q: If I can think of what the name of the school was Steubenville (phonetic) High School. Steubenville Stupidsville High School.

99.t: School vocal music, glee club and Mrs. Hewey
99.s: Asked about his earlier music, he explains he had only vocal solfege and glee club singing, encouraged by teacher Mrs. Hewey.

99.s: He briefly changes to Gibbs High in Little Rock hoping to join a school band, finds he must own an instrument, and returns home as tuition begins.

115.t: Glee Club and his Houston high schools
115.s: He sang in the Glee Club, and describes Gregory, Booker T. Washington and Jack Yates schools, where he also took music lessons.
115.ch: Childhood in Tyler, Beaumont and Houston
115.q: Because when I got into high school in Houston, I left Gregory and got promoted and went to high school, which was Booker Washington.

115.t: Flunking a year of high school; the Glee Club and Professor Jackson
115.s: He stayed back a year over a missing notebook and sang in the Glee Club under A. S. Jackson, who made students sing notes before they could play.
115.q: I had to stay in one year because I didn't have a notebook. As I said, it was three of us that had to stay in my class. It was Ruth Love and John Collins.

75.t: Growing up on 63rd Street, Catholic school and confirmation
75.s: He was raised on 63rd Street, attended the Henrietta School and Catholic church (St. Benedict the Moor), was confirmed by Bishop Hayes, and later moved to Manhattan Avenue in Harlem.
75.q: : Yeah. I was raised there. I went to the school, the Henrietta School, which was the Children's Aid Society. They have records there; I have all the records.

75.t: Spanish, English teachers and schools up to Cooper High
75.s: He understood Spanish but thought in English, taught by English teachers, and moved through P.S. schools to James Fenimore Cooper, from an Irish to a Jewish neighborhood.
75.q: Oh yeah. It will come back, you know. But I was taught English by English teachers. Campbell, Morrissey. In those days, the teachers were... There were very few Jewish teachers, like they have... They have command of this education today. But then I had Gloria...Miss Campbell... I had all kinds...…

171.t: Leaving Austin in 1932 for Western University and working his way through
171.s: He left August 1932 on a music scholarship to Western University in Kansas, working odd jobs and painting buildings.
171.ch: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
171.q: Yeah. But I had an uncle named Calvin who was a painter by trade, house painter by trade. He had taught me painting. So when I got to Western University, a friend of mine, Emmett Lindsay and I, not only did we take over the furnace room and handle those big boilers (in the) boiler room, but we also…

171.t: Gus Johnson's Texas and Kansas City background
171.s: Gus came from Texas, attended Sumner High and Junior College, then went to Omaha.
171.ch: Europe, the bank and Kansas City revisited

79.t: Summers home; the capitol dedication in Jefferson City
79.s: Thomas completed four years, went home each summer, and the band was away three days for the dedication of the new capitol.
79.q: Well, that's a funny thing that you asked me about that. Yes, I would go home each summer but during some of these times, like the dedication of the capital, we were out for three days.

79.t: What marching taught; studies, baseball and tennis
79.s: Thomas says marching taught respect for the instrument and the conductor. He was a good student who also played baseball and tennis.
79.q: Yeah, tremendous. You have a chance to know respect for the instrument. You have a chance to know respect for the conductor and the guys right there with you. And, it's a beautiful experience.

174.t: Schools attended and music in school
174.s: He lists his Catholic and public schools, a piano-playing teacher, and says school offered singing but no music reading he recalls.
174.q: Well that was an everyday occurrence, you know, singing because you're singing maybe in the morning.

175.t: Living across from the halls; schools and Xavier
175.s: He lived opposite the halls, heard players like Piron, and lists the schools he attended through 1934 and a year at Xavier.
175.q: As a matter of fact, I used to stay right across the street from there, so therefore I had access to the places at various times of the day, and where I'd get a chance to listen to some of the fellas playing and whatnot. And I think it was one of these halls, which when I don't remember, that I got…

769.s: He attended school at Franklin and Perdido and McDonogh 24 through the fifth grade, then went to work.
769.q: This fellow, Henry Martin, that I was telling you about, that was his mother's place. Oh, I see. She was taking care of it there. And I went to that school and when we moved up from Calton, I went to MacDonald number 24. I went as far to fifth grade. I played hookah so the old lady pulled me out…

457.t: Early schooling: Nelson Academy and Southern University
457.s: He attended a private school next door to his birthplace, as his father rejected public schools.
457.q: Yeah, it was a private institution. And the Southern University- See, my father at that time didn't believe in sending us to public schools. My brother and I both finished there.

181.t: Labor Day parades and Parker's sister's schooling
181.s: Not enough bands for Labor Day, so country bands filled out the parade; Parker never schooled in New Orleans, his sister did.
181.q: Oh, man. They didn't have bands enough to furnish the companies. Oh, bands. Set out in the country and get them country bands. Come fill out the parade.

32.t: Leaving Benedict College after drinking with Pinckney's band
32.s: White names the band's directors, then tells how Benedict's president told him to leave because he took a drink while playing with Tom Pinckney's band.
32.q: Four years of age. Four years of age. Little Sammy Coates directed the band as a comedy director, however. Yes. Under me, under Hardy, under John Brown, and under Brooks Brockman. Brooks Brockman lived in Los Angeles until about three years ago, and he died. Now, I'm leaving the Jenkins orphanage…

955.s: He went to Catholic school and St. Catherine School on Tulane Avenue.
955.q: Yeah, well, I come up through Catholic school. I used to go to Miss Jeanette until I made my first communion. And after I made first communion, my mother continued with the St. Catherine School.

252.t: First coming to New Orleans: schools and moving back and forth from Mobile
252.s: Diggs remembers arriving in New Orleans at five, school with white teachers, a second stay at 12-13, and returning for good after the storm; Boote adds she was born in Mobile.
252.ch: Growing up between Mobile and New Orleans
252.q: Mm-hmm. How do you remember? When I first come to New Orleans, I was five years old. When I first come to New Orleans, I was five years old. When I first come to New Orleans, I was five years old.

I've been known his, his father and this kid, he was seven years old at that time. That's from the East, I guess. Yeah,…

848.t: Southern University and Kimball's own schools
848.s: Discussion of the Southern University and New Orleans University schools; Kimball's own schooling at James Lewis, McDonogh 35 and New Orleans University.
848.ch: Henry Kimball and the Kimball family
848.q: Yes, that was, that was called Southern University. Southern University. Oh, I had Southern University. Both my mother and he attended that school. Yes.

1023.t: Warren Easton school band and the Armistice Day strike
1023.s: He recalls teacher Mike Capera, a student strike on Armistice Day, and the school band whose members later turned professional. Louis Prima was not in it.
1023.q: Well, I went to Warren Easton and Mike Capera was the music teacher out there. And at that time, he didn't like me at all. I should mention that. And when I came into a certain misfortune at one time, he read it out and practically told the class, see if you guys don't behave yourselves, you'll do…

172.t: Schooling and listening to a 1960 old-style band recording
172.s: A question about school goes unanswered; Ridgley hears a June 1960 recording with Peter Bocage and Charlie Love and calls it the old style.
172.q: That's like Bob Lyons and Frankie Deucing. That's like Bob Lyons and Frankie Deucing. Yeah, that's way back there. That's the old style way back on the center. They might not be an old musician, but it's sound.

257.t: Carpet Christie, Xavier and school bands
257.s: They compare school bands at Carpet Christie, Xavier high school and college, and St. Augustine.
257.ch: Music scene, school and father's advice
257.q: I don't know, Bill. I don't know, to tell you the truth. I mean, that I remember, because I'm born and raised right up there. I'm pretty, you know, a member of the church.

262.t: McNeil's school band at Lafon and its alumni
262.s: McNeil moved between New Orleans and Chicago, then joined the first Negro school band under Valmo Victor; alumni like Joe Newman are discussed.

251.t: Catholic school, Jones school, Straight University and self-education
251.s: Albert lists his schools, says he left college studies to play music, claims a high school degree, and says he educated himself through contacts and reading.

It was a block around there just to be with the kids and the teachers seemed to like me and I could go into rooms. and then after I left Catholic…

126.t: School, Tulane and unpaid fraternity dances
126.s: The band attended high school and Tulane together, played fraternity and sorority dances for ice cream and cake, never for pay.
126.q: Well, we all went to the local high school for a year or two, and the third and fourth years of my high school education was spent at Manual Training School, which is Dr. Souchon and Gibbons attended as well. Then, of course, after getting out of high school, we all went to Tulane.

448.t: Eastman for one term, then returning to study with Bechet

42.t: Coming to Tulane as a graduate student and teaching

277.t: Jazz Limited, Sidney Bechet, and school work suffering
277.s: He frequented Jazz Limited, preferred Dodds to Bechet, and his schoolwork suffered so he left after a year.
277.q: I used to go there quite a lot because I knew people who were working there like Don Yule and Dick Wells did. I used to like to hear Sidney Bechet who was working there for a while.

46.t: Being made to write right-handed at school
46.s: Chicago teachers switched him to writing right-handed, unlike his school in New Orleans; he never stuttered.
46.q: Well, no, I don't write left-handed. That's the funny thing. When I went to school in Chicago, in those days, the teachers used to make you change hands. Now they don't do it with my kid. I mean, they say, if you left-handed, well, he's naturally left-handed like I was. And they don't change him.…

278.t: Booker T. Washington High School and schoolmates
278.s: He says he registered at one school but attended Booker T. with James Rivers.
278.q: Not green school, I don't think. I registered for a green school one year. I think it was when it was, well, I don't know what was going on during that period, but it was some sort of transitional period going on. And I registered, but I didn't go to that school green. 631.t: Jackson School and music in school
631.s: He went to Jackson School c. 1905 with future musicians in the school orchestra; music taught briefly by blackboard.
631.q: No. That'd be about, uh, 1905, I guess. Something like that. Of course, you see, the first day I had, my, I was taught at home by my sisters. Oh, they did? Give me a fortune. First day I went to school, I went to third grade. Ah. And the third grade was a lot more severe in those days than it is…

And I moved from there to 4530 South Robinson Street. And from 4530 South Robinson Street, that's where I attended…

724.s: Raised indoors near Semperm, he attended a private Catholic school.
724.ch: Childhood, Mardi Gras and first brass band
724.q: My first school was a private school, just about, just a block and a half from where I was living. Because after I was born and grew up big enough to go to school, we was living on the island between Johnson and Galvis. Was it one of the Catholic schools? Yes. That was the first school I went to,…

47.t: Cincinnati, Indiana dance halls and Hoagy at Indiana University
47.s: Tiger Rag nightly, Cincinnati bands, a tough Indiana dance hall contract, and Hoagy's long years at Indiana University.

121.t: Choosing Greenwald School of Music on the GI Bill
121.s: After considering the Navy and barber college he enrolled at Greenwald, taught by college faculty; alumni include Red Tyler and Earl Palmer.
121.q: I would sing, you know. But, um, and musically, I would think of that. First of all, first of all, first of all, first I started to go to, uh, I would sing, you know.

665.s: She left Natchez College when her father died; side chatter with a peach seller.
665.q: Yeah. He was just like you see me. He wouldn't fix himself up or nothing. That old man had a head on him. He used to work with the papers too.
